title: Chatbots flunk retirement advice test: Actuaries Institute
full_text:
Chatbots flunk retirement advice test: Actuaries InstituteBY RIDDHIMA TALWANI | MONDAY, 16 NOV 2026 12:19PMThe Actuaries Institute said while artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to democratise financial advice, it needs to be well regulated, controlled and governed. In its discussion paper, How AI can help people make better financial decisions: Improving access to financial help, guidance and advice, the institute sets out four practical areas for action that could help combat the shortcomings of existing chatbots and AI tools. In the research, the authors tested four popular chatbots using five hypothetical Australian retirement and investment scenarios. The authors found while the chatbots made some acceptable recommendations, most responses were potentially incomplete or potentially inappropriate. "Many people turn to chatbots for financial advice because they seem like the easiest option, but most people lack the financial experience and expertise to ask the right questions in the right way," Actuaries Institute public policy council committee member and actuary Nathan Bonarius said. "Chatbots can confidently make inconsistent or incorrect recommendations that appear to be personal advice, even if there are disclaimers." Bonarius added all four models failed the detailed query about retirement. "What is most concerning is that all four failed the most consequential question in our testing - a detailed query about retirement advice - at a time when one in eight over-45s use AI for super and retirement questions," he said. The discussion paper found popular chatbots and existing AI-enabled advice models struggled to perform calculations, projections and scenario modelling. Responses were difficult to explain and audit. It is also unclear where liability should lie for errors or poor-quality AI-generated financial advice. "AI has been developing quickly but the rules haven't caught up. We need to work together to create the right environment for AI-enabled financial advice to provide quality financial help, guidance and advice to millions of Australians who are currently locked out of accessing personalised support," Bonarius said. The report suggests four areas to drive better AI-enabled help, guidance and advice: raising financial capability, digital literacy and AI literacy, encouraging innovation in financial services, updating regulations and enforcement to allow for emerging developments in AI and strengthen regulators' AI capabilities. "Our longer-term aspiration is for all Australians to have access to trusted help, guidance and advice, including through AI. Getting there won't be simple, but the opportunity is significant: affordable, personalised support when people face important financial decisions," Actuaries Institute chief executive Elayne Grace said. "Progress will depend on working together to lift consumers' financial and AI literacy, give responsible providers room to innovate, and strengthen regulation and supervision so consumers are protected. Actuaries can help support innovation and build trust by designing and testing AI-enabled advice, drawing on their expertise in modelling, risk and governance, with a focus on good outcomes for consumers."
